name: fastfilter (hexops)
workload: populate() and contains() on 1M-100M random u64 keys, comparing binaryfuse8/16/32 vs xor2/4/8/16/32 vs fuse (Zig implementation, zig run -O ReleaseFast src/benchmark.zig)
claimed_speedup: binaryfuse8 populates 1M keys in 37.5ms vs xor8's 103.4ms (~2.7x faster construction, i9-9900K-class Mac) and ~19x-4x faster at 100M keys (7.4s vs 28.0s); contains() latency roughly equal to xor filter (~24ns) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: zig run -O ReleaseFast src/benchmark.zig -- --xor 8 --num-keys N; Zig 0.12.0-dev.706+62a0fbdae
hardware: 2019 MacBook Pro, 2.3GHz 8-core Intel i9, 16GB DDR4 (also tested on AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, Windows 10)
stars_or_usage: 293 stars (archived GitHub mirror; project now self-hosted on Forgejo)
tradeoffs: Zig-only (not directly usable from C/C++ without a C ABI shim); iterator-based population reduces memory; larger fingerprint widths (u16/u32) trade memory for lower false-positive rate; GitHub mirror is archived, canonical repo moved to project's own Forgejo instance
caveats: The repo's own benchmark table compares binary-fuse/xor/fuse variants against each other, not against a classic bit-array Bloom filter or cuckoo filter directly (the 'faster than Bloom/smaller than Cuckoo' claim in the README is a general characterization of the algorithm family, not a number measured in this repo's own harness); originally on GitHub (hexops/xorfilter, hexops/fastfilter) which now just redirects, canonical source is now code.hexops.org
found_via: Blogs / talks: HN Algolia query "fastfilter" surfaced 'Show HN: Fastfilter: Binary fuse and xor filters for Zig' (2023-06-02, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=36148002-equivalent thread) -> opened project README

name: autoscale_cuckoo_filter
baseline: cuckoo filter (sile/cuckoo_filter and ZePedroResende/cuckoo_filter, and the `cuckoofilter` crate)
workload: contains/add/remove ops/sec on 100,000 items, capacity=200,000, target FPP~1%, comparing against two other Rust Cuckoo Filter crates
claimed_speedup: 77.32 M/s contains (vs 17.23 M/s and 23.87 M/s for the two comparison crates, ~3.2-4.5x), 31.25 M/s add (~1.3-3x), 48.36 M/s remove (~2.3-2.8x); README markets this as '4.5x faster lookups, 3x faster additions/removals'
tradeoffs: cuckoo filter caveats apply (deletion can cause false negatives on double-delete/never-inserted keys, documented at length in README); part of a monorepo, not a standalone repo; comparison crates chosen by the author, not the canonical CMU cuckoo filter C++ reference
caveats: No compiler flags or CPU model stated for the benchmark table, so capped at Tier C; README claims it is 'Forked from sile/cuckoo_filter' but that exact repo name no longer resolves on GitHub (a similarly-named sile/scalable_cuckoo_filter and a separate ZePedroResende/cuckoo_filter crate both exist), so the fork parent could not be confirmed precisely -- left as null rather than guessed
found_via: Blogs / talks: HN Algolia query "cuckoo filter rust" surfaced 'Fastest Auto-Scaling Cuckoo Filter in Rust (v0.5.8)' (2025-12-30, crates.io listing) -> opened crates.io page and GitHub README

name: Modern Bloom Filters (save-buffer benchmark suite)
workload: insert/query cycles-per-op on random 64-bit hashes at 1% target FPR, progressing from a naive Bloom filter through blocked, register-blocked/SIMD (AVX2), and bit-pattern (with mask rotation) variants
claimed_speedup: naive Bloom filter: ~56-254 cycles/op -> blocked: ~30 cycles/op -> register-blocked AVX2: ~5 cycles/op (4x faster than the non-SIMD register-blocked version) -> bit-pattern SIMD ('ultimate' filter): ~2.5 cycles/op, a 22x overall throughput increase over the classic Bloom filter
tradeoffs: the fastest variant trades a higher, less predictable false-positive rate and requires AVX2; bit-pattern approach needs a precomputed mask table
caveats: Underlying repo (save-buffer/bloomfilter_benchmarks) is on the excluded KNOWN_LIST, but this blog post is a first-party Tier-A benchmark write-up (public code, compiler+flags+CPU stated) for that known project, so reported per the exception rule with is_evidence_for_known=true; blog's own GitHub Pages URL (save-buffer.github.io/bloom_filter.html) permanently redirects to blog.krassovsky.com, the author's personal domain -- both opened and confirmed identical content
found_via: Blogs / talks: HN Algolia query "bloom filter faster" surfaced 'Modern Bloom Filters: 22x Faster' (2023-05-30) -> opened blog post directly
